title: Biased random walks on small-world networks
shortTitle: When drift speeds up a small world
oneLine: Candidate proof of the stated AIM mixing bounds for four fixed-weight clock conventions: logarithmic in the denser regime, square-root up to polylogarithmic factors in the sparser regime.
abstract: A cycle with independent undirected shortcuts and fixed forward and backward weights admits a candidate worst-start mixing theorem under four explicit clocks. At shortcut probability epsilon/n the mixing order is logarithmic; at epsilon n^(-3/2), the bounds run from c sqrt(n) log n to C sqrt(n)(log n)^18. The proof keeps random spacing, physical crossing durations, exceptional starts and parity separate. Exact rational tests corroborate finite identities only.
narration: Imagine walking around a ring of locations, with occasional shortcuts joining distant points. A short route across the network does not automatically mean a random walker quickly forgets where it started. This candidate asks what changes when movement around the ring has a fixed directional bias. The written proof gives two answers for an explicitly defined random network. With the larger shortcut density, the claimed mixing time grows only logarithmically with the number of locations. With fewer shortcuts, it grows on a square-root scale, up to logarithmic factors. The sparse upper and lower bounds do not match exactly. The argument covers four ways of measuring time, including a discrete walk that never deliberately stays still. Several obstacles matter. Fast mixing among shortcut endpoints can hide slow movement between them. Travel duration and destination are dependent. An average starting point is not the worst starting point. And a nonlazy walk can retain an even-odd obstruction. The proof treats each issue separately using random spacing, joint clock estimates and parity control. Readers can inspect the detailed proof modules and rerun exact rational checks of finite matrix identities. Those checks do not certify the asymptotic theorem. The weights and directional bias are fixed as the network grows; arbitrary weight rules and vanishing bias are excluded. This is an unrefereed Evidence Press candidate dated September eighth, twenty twenty-six. The full paper, code and evidence are linked on the release page. This is an AI-generated voice summary, not additional mathematical evidence.

keyResults: Worst-start Theta(log n) mixing in the denser bounded-average-degree regime.
Sparse lower c sqrt(n) log n and upper C sqrt(n)(log n)^18, with high probability.
Four fixed-weight clocks, including nonlazy discrete time with explicit parity analysis.
A consolidated dimension-uniform clock–endpoint renewal statement with stationary moments.
evidence: Seven-page entry-point paper; detailed proof modules; standard-library exact matrix checks; normal, optimized and fresh-archive replay; three semantic mutants; source comparison and internal editorial reports.
statusDetail: Unrefereed candidate proof for four fixed-weight clocks. Sparse bounds differ by polylogarithmic factors. No vanishing drift, arbitrary kernel, historical priority, external specialist validation, formal verification or impact claim.
